|BOX 2 Making a diagnosis of egg allergy

• Most children should receive a clinical diagnosis without resorting to food challenge.
• If the history is unclear, a negative skin prick test can exclude egg allergy.
• Skin prick test weal size or level of specific IgE does not predict the severity of allergic reactions to egg29.
• The severity of a reaction depends on the amount of allergen ingested, the matrix, how well it is cooked and concomitant asthma, exercise or illness.
| |---| #### 5 | CLINICAL PRESENTATION AND SEVERITY The onset of egg allergy is usually observed early in life, in children with eczema and atopy. Egg allergy most commonly presents after the first apparent ingestion.8,10,11 Most reactions occur to lightly cooked egg, with reactions to baked egg and raw egg being less common.10 Clinical reactions include urticaria and/or angio-oedema in 80–90% (within minutes) and gastrointestinal symptoms in 10–44% (within 2 h).10,12–14 Most reactions occurring in the community are mild, with facial erythema and/or urticaria. In children, a mild reaction is characterized by cutaneous symptoms on significant exposure (e.g. a mouthful of cooked egg) sometimes associated with a single vomit. A hoarse cry, change in voice pitch, cough, stridor or wheeze indicates involvement of the respiratory tract and a more severe reaction. Occasionally young children develop pallor and floppiness. Moderate to severe reactions with respiratory symptoms are less common; 5–10% in challenge studies, but less in the community, where the initial triggering dose is usually lower.10,12,13 Prior to presentation to allergy services, anaphylaxis occurs in 7%.10

Adult-onset egg allergy may be:

- 1. New onset adult egg allergy after eggs have been tolerated for years.71
- 2. Part of the bird-egg syndrome (a combination of bird-feather sensitization and egg allergy) with an allergy to egg yolk. ‘Bird egg syndrome’ was originally described in subjects, mainly women, who were sensitized to egg yolk and bird (budgerigar and hen) feathers.72 This syndrome is seen in subjects who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.73 The allergen responsible is alpha livetin (chicken serum albumin, Gal d 5), found in large amounts in egg yolk.74 Typically, patients develop upper and lower respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds and gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Patients should receive egg avoidance advice, emergency medication and be trained in its use.
- 3. Occupational, for example, in workers from the baking industry, who develop sensitization by inhalation.75


There is little information on the prognosis of adult egg allergy and patients should be seen periodically to repeat specific IgE and to update training in the use of emergency medication. Older children or adults with a pre-existing egg allergy, presenting to the adult clinic for the first time, should be assessed for the likely resolution of egg allergy. Component testing can be useful in determining whether an OFC is feasible, with a negative test to Gal d 1 (ovomucoid), suggesting that a baked egg challenge might be tolerated. Although systematic review data suggest that 30% of egg-allergic children will continue to have persisting egg allergy after the age of 16 years, there are no data on continued resolution in young adults. Clinical experience shows that although it persists in some and may be lifelong, many others may have partly or wholly resolving egg allergy, even in their late 20' s. It is extremely important to establish the likelihood of tolerance with oral food challenges, as reactions can be severe and fatal anaphylaxis to egg has been reported in an adult patient.76

- 11 | OTHER EGG-RELATED CONDITIONS

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Egg allergy
  Synonyms:
    - Hen's egg allergy
    - IgE-mediated egg allergy
    - Type-1 hypersensitivity to egg
  Description: An adverse immunologic reaction to egg proteins, primarily ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and ovomucoid (Gal d 1), mediated by specific IgE antibodies. The reaction is typically immediate type-1 hypersensitivity with rapid symptom onset; late-phase and delayed hypersensitivity reactions can also occur, particularly in the context of eczema.
  Epidemiology: Prevalence is approximately 2% in children and 0.1% in adults in the United Kingdom. Onset most commonly occurs in infancy, often after the first apparent ingestion; new-onset egg allergy in adults is rare.
  Clinical presentation: Typical presentation is in infancy, with rapid onset (within minutes) of cutaneous symptoms (erythema, urticaria, angioedema) and/or vomiting following egg ingestion. Severe reactions are less common and may involve respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, breathing difficulty) or cardiovascular symptoms (pallor, floppiness). Reaction severity is influenced by the amount of egg ingested and the degree of cooking; raw egg white is the most allergenic form. Delayed worsening of eczema may also occur.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Childhood-onset egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Usually presents in infancy, often with mild to moderate symptoms; high rate of spontaneous resolution by adolescence; commonly associated with other atopic conditions such as eczema and asthma.
    - Name: Adult-onset egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Rare; may occur as new onset in adulthood after years of tolerance, or as persistence of childhood allergy; tends to be more severe and persistent; can be associated with bird-egg syndrome or occupational sensitization.
    - Name: Occupational egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Results from inhalation of egg protein aerosols in occupational settings (e.g., baking industry); may develop respiratory symptoms and subsequently react upon ingestion.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To establish a diagnosis of egg allergy based on typical symptoms.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected egg allergy.
      Interpretation: Rapid onset (minutes) of erythema, urticaria, angioedema, and/or vomiting after egg ingestion is highly suggestive. Mild reactions in a clear history are sufficient for diagnosis without further testing.
    - Test: Skin prick test (SPT) with standardized whole egg reagent
      Purpose: To confirm IgE sensitization to egg.
      When indicated: Moderate‑severe reactions, or when the clinical history is unclear.
      Interpretation: A weal size of ≥3 mm in combination with a supportive clinical history is diagnostic in most cases. Higher cut‑offs (e.g., ≥5 mm in children under 2 years) increase specificity. SPT weal size does not predict clinical severity. SPT should not be used for screening in the absence of suspected reaction.
    - Test: Egg‑specific IgE assay (serum)
      Purpose: To detect circulating egg‑specific IgE antibodies.
      When indicated: When SPT is unavailable, or in moderate‑severe cases to support diagnosis.
      Interpretation: No single diagnostic cut‑off value is applicable across all ages; low levels can be found in egg‑tolerant children. Therefore, results must be correlated with clinical history. Egg‑specific IgE should not be measured in asymptomatic individuals as it may lead to unnecessary dietary restriction.
    - Test: Component‑resolved diagnostics (specific IgE to Gal d 1, Gal d 2, Gal d 3, Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify sensitization to individual egg allergens, which aids in predicting persistence and tolerance to baked egg.
      When indicated: When assessing likelihood of resolution, especially in older children or adults; may guide decisions on oral food challenge.
      Interpretation: Sensitization to multiple components, particularly Gal d 1 (ovomucoid), suggests persistent allergy. Negative Gal d 1 IgE is associated with a higher chance of tolerating baked egg. Ovalbumin (Gal d 2) IgE is common but less predictive of severity. Gal d 5 indicates egg yolk allergy and possible bird‑egg syndrome.
    - Test: Oral food challenge (OFC)
      Purpose: To definitively confirm or refute the diagnosis, or to prove tolerance has developed.
      When indicated: When clinical history and test results are discordant, or to assess resolution of allergy. Hospital‑based challenges are reserved for high‑risk patients (Box 4).
      Interpretation: A controlled graded ingestion of egg (baked, lightly cooked, or raw) under medical supervision; positive if objective allergic symptoms occur. Baked egg challenges are used to determine if heat‑processed egg is tolerated.
    - Test: Prick‑to‑prick testing with raw egg
      Purpose: To detect sensitization to raw egg proteins.
      When indicated: Not routinely recommended; may be considered in research settings.
      Interpretation: A weal of ≥13 mm has been reported as diagnostic. Does not predict baked egg tolerance and carries a risk of systemic reaction; not standardized.
    - Test: Skin prick test with baked egg slurry
      Purpose: To predict the outcome of a baked egg challenge.
      When indicated: Research setting; not routinely used in clinical practice.
      Interpretation: High negative predictive value reported in one study.
    - Test: Peanut‑specific IgE (co‑testing)
      Purpose: To assess risk of peanut allergy and guide early peanut introduction advice.
      When indicated: Infants with moderate‑severe egg allergy.
      Interpretation: Egg allergy in infancy is associated with increased risk of peanut allergy; early peanut introduction may prevent its development.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Egg white‑specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Indicates sensitization to egg white proteins; supports clinical diagnosis when history is positive but not diagnostic in isolation.
    - Marker: Ovalbumin (Gal d 2) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Major heat‑labile egg white allergen; commonly detected in egg‑allergic individuals.
    - Marker: Ovomucoid (Gal d 1) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable or elevated
      Clinical significance: Heat‑stable and immunodominant allergen; sensitization is associated with persistent egg allergy, greater severity, and reduced likelihood of baked egg tolerance.
    - Marker: Gal d 3 specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Egg white allergen; may contribute to sensitization profile.
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Egg yolk allergen; marker for bird‑egg syndrome; indicates cross‑reactivity with bird feather allergens.
    - Marker: Skin prick test weal diameter (to egg white)
      Expected result: ≥3 mm
      Clinical significance: Supports diagnosis of egg allergy when combined with history; larger weals increase specificity but do not correlate with severity.
  Prognostic tools:
    - Name: Prognostic indicators for resolution of egg allergy
      Components:
      - Age at tolerance to baked egg
      - Reaction severity (mild/cutaneous only vs respiratory/multisystem)
      - Presence of asthma
      - Severity of eczema
      - Egg‑specific IgE level
      - Sensitization to multiple egg allergen components (especially ovomucoid/Gal d 1)
      - Number of co‑existing food allergies
      - Atopic comorbidities
      Risk groups:
      - Group: Favorable prognosis
      Criteria: Mild or cutaneous‑only initial reactions, no asthma, low egg‑specific IgE, early tolerance of baked egg, absence of ovomucoid or multi‑component sensitization, and no other food allergies or severe eczema.
      Expected outcome: High likelihood of outgrowing allergy; median age of resolution for well‑cooked egg is 67 months and for uncooked egg 127 months; approximately 68% resolve by 16 years.
      - Group: Unfavorable prognosis
      Criteria: History of respiratory or cardiovascular severe reactions, presence of asthma or severe eczema, high egg‑specific IgE, sensitization to multiple components (especially ovomucoid), and multiple food allergies.
      Expected outcome: More likely to have persistent allergy into adolescence or adulthood; delayed achievement of tolerance to well‑cooked egg and uncooked egg.
      Interpretation: These factors guide the timing and setting of egg reintroduction (home vs hospital) and the need for specialist allergy follow‑up. Children with favorable features may attempt home‑based baked egg introduction from 12 months.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: All infants and young children with egg allergy should be periodically assessed for suitability of reintroduction. Adults and older children with persistent egg allergy should be reviewed at intervals to update emergency medication training, repeat specific IgE testing, and consider component testing and oral food challenges to determine if resolution has occurred. Exact frequency is not specified but typically annual or as guided by clinical progress.
    Recommended tests:
      - Interval clinical history (new reactions, dietary adherence, growth)
      - Egg‑specific IgE (and possibly component IgE) to monitor sensitization trends
      - Skin prick testing when appropriate
      - Consideration of oral food challenge to baked egg or cooked egg when prognostic factors are favorable
    Long term effects:
      - Risk of accidental anaphylaxis, including fatalities
      - Dietary restrictions impacting quality of life and social participation
      - Psychosocial burden: anxiety, bullying, family stress
      - Potential for nutritional deficiencies if multiple food allergies
      - In persistent cases, lifelong egg avoidance may be required
    Survivorship notes: Many children outgrow egg allergy; early introduction of baked egg may accelerate tolerance. Adults with persistent allergy should receive ongoing support and education. All patients need an up‑to‑date emergency management plan and ready access to antihistamines and adrenaline auto‑injectors.

SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23. Skin prick testing using a slurry of baked egg had a high negative predictive value for a negative baked egg challenge in one study.24 It is not routinely used in clinical practice.

question: ¿Cómo debe interpretarse Component‑resolved diagnostics (specific IgE to Gal d 1, Gal d 2, Gal d 3, Gal d 5) según la guía?
gold_answer: Sensitization to multiple components, particularly Gal d 1 (ovomucoid), suggests persistent allergy. Negative Gal d 1 IgE is associated with a higher chance of tolerating baked egg. Supervised baked egg challenge should be using a one egg per eight fairy cake recipes in the first instance. There may be exceptions, for example, if a child has had a subsequent mild reaction after significant accidental exposure. Children on biologics for asthma should be considered for food challenge once their asthma control has improved. #### 9.6 | Oral immunotherapy Egg immunotherapy is a deliberate attempt, using regular ingestion of egg, usually with increasing amounts, to generate tolerance to egg in a patient with established egg allergy (usually over 5 years of age). Several studies have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of egg oral immunotherapy (OIT).22,59–62 It is time consuming for clinicians and requires significant commitment for families. Desensitization occurs, although tolerance may not be maintained after withdrawal of treatment. A Cochrane review in 2018 commented that studies were small, and the quality of evidence is low.63,64 There are no standardized protocols and a high incidence of adverse events.63,65 In one study, adrenaline was required in 26% of children.65 Early discontinuation is associated with underlying asthma, higher specific IgE and lower threshold during double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge.65 Ovomucoid IgE >8.85 kU/L indicated a 95% probability of early discontinuation or ongoing reactions over time.65 More recent protocols achieve tolerance in 50% of patients.60,66 The benefits are sustained for up to 5 years after treatment.66 Daily dosing is more effective than weekly dosing.67 Low pre-treatment levels of egg white and ovomucoid IgE predict sustained unresponsiveness following egg immunotherapy.68 Decrease in size of SPT and increase in egg-specific IgG4 over time predicts tolerance in children being treated with egg OIT.61 Ovalbumin IgG4 and Ovalbumin IgE/ IgG4 ratio may be useful to predict the development of tolerance to egg in oral immunotherapy.65 EAACI does not currently recommend egg OIT as a treatment to achieve long-term tolerance in children with persistent egg allergy.69

Clinical experience shows that although it persists in some and may be lifelong, many others may have partly or wholly resolving egg allergy, even in their late 20' s. - 11 | OTHER EGG-RELATED CONDITIONS


- 11.1 | Egg allergy and asthma


Children with egg allergy are at increased risk of other allergic diseases especially asthma (odds ratio 5.0).77 A careful history should, therefore, be taken to enquire about respiratory symptoms. The presence of asthma may increase the potential severity

of accidental egg reactions and excellent asthma control should be a priority. #### 11.2 | Egg allergy as a risk factor for peanut allergy

Infants with egg allergy are at risk of developing peanut allergy.

Children on biologics for asthma should be considered for food challenge once their asthma control has improved. #### 9.6 | Oral immunotherapy

Egg immunotherapy is a deliberate attempt, using regular ingestion of egg, usually with increasing amounts, to generate tolerance to egg in a patient with established egg allergy (usually over 5 years of age). Several studies have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of egg oral immunotherapy (OIT).22,59–62 It is time consuming for clinicians and requires significant commitment for families. Desensitization occurs, although tolerance may not be maintained after withdrawal of treatment. A Cochrane review in 2018 commented that studies were small, and the quality of evidence is low.63,64 There are no standardized protocols and a high incidence of adverse events.63,65 In one study, adrenaline was required in 26% of children.65 Early discontinuation is associated with underlying asthma, higher specific IgE and lower threshold during double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge.65 Ovomucoid IgE >8.85 kU/L indicated a 95% probability of early discontinuation or ongoing reactions over time.65

More recent protocols achieve tolerance in 50% of patients.60,66 The benefits are sustained for up to 5 years after treatment.66 Daily dosing is more effective than weekly dosing.67 Low pre-treatment levels of egg white and ovomucoid IgE predict sustained unresponsiveness following egg immunotherapy.68 Decrease in size of SPT and increase in egg-specific IgG4 over time predicts tolerance in children being treated with egg OIT.61 Ovalbumin IgG4 and Ovalbumin IgE/ IgG4 ratio may be useful to predict the development of tolerance to egg in oral immunotherapy.65

EAACI does not currently recommend egg OIT as a treatment to achieve long-term tolerance in children with persistent egg allergy.69 Egg oral immunotherapy should only be undertaken in highly specialized allergy centres.69

question: ¿Cómo debe interpretarse Oral food challenge (OFC) según la guía?

Investigation by measuring egg-specific IgE (by skin prick testing or specific IgE assay) is useful in moderate-severe cases or where there is diagnostic uncertainty. #### 2 | DEFINITION AND MECHANISM

Egg allergy is an adverse immunological reaction, most often induced by the proteins in egg white, usually ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and/ or ovomucoid (Gal d 1) mediated by egg-specific IgE. - 7.2 | Egg-specific IgE


When skin prick testing is not available, measurement of eggspecific IgE may be carried out in patients with a history of moderate/severe reactions to egg containing food, to confirm a clinical suspicion of egg allergy. Low levels of egg-specific IgE may be found in children without clinical egg allergy.13 The measurement of egg-specific IgE in the absence of a history of egg ingestion is discouraged as, in this circumstance, the test has poor specificity and low negative predictive value; cautious home introduction or oral challenge will subsequently be required if the egg-specific IgE level is positive but low.8 Measurement of peanut-specific IgE should be included in infants with moderate/severe egg allergy to guide peanut allergy prevention advice.25

#### 7.3 | Egg component testing

The egg white components are ovomucoid (Gal d 1), ovalbumin (Gal d 2), ovotransferrin (Gal d 3), lysozyme (Gal d 4) and livetin (Gal d 5). Adults with persistence of childhood egg allergy have more sequential than conformational IgE epitopes of ovomucoid.70

question: ¿Cómo define la guía Bird‑egg syndrome?
gold_answer: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.

retrieved_chunks.text: ‘Bird egg syndrome’ was originally described in subjects, mainly women, who were sensitized to egg yolk and bird (budgerigar and hen) feathers.72 This syndrome is seen in subjects who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.73 The allergen responsible is alpha livetin (chicken serum albumin, Gal d 5), found in large amounts in egg yolk.74 Typically, patients develop upper and lower respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds and gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Egg yolk alpha-livetin (chicken serum albumin) is a cross-reactive allergen in the bird-egg syndrome. Chicken serum albumin (Gal d 5*) is a partially heatlabile inhalant and food allergen implicated in the bird-egg syndrome.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Bird‑egg syndrome
  Synonyms:
    - Alpha‑livetin allergy
    - Egg yolk allergy with bird feather sensitization
  Description: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.
  Epidemiology: Rare; described mainly in adults, particularly women, with prolonged exposure to budgerigars, pigeons, or other caged birds.
  Clinical presentation: Upper and lower respiratory symptoms (rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma) on inhalation of bird allergens; gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Symptoms are triggered by ingestion of egg yolk, which contains high concentrations of alpha‑livetin. Onset typically after years of bird exposure.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To identify the characteristic cross‑reactivity between bird and egg allergens.
      When indicated: Suspected cases with respiratory symptoms on bird exposure and food reactions to egg yolk.
      Interpretation: A history of bird feather sensitivity and symptoms with egg (especially yolk) or chicken meat is highly suggestive.
    - Test: Skin prick test or specific IgE to egg yolk
      Purpose: To confirm sensitization to egg yolk proteins.
      When indicated: When bird‑egg syndrome is suspected.
      Interpretation: Positive test indicates sensitization to yolk allergen; further distinction can be made with component testing.
    - Test: Specific IgE to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify the specific cross‑reactive allergen.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected bird‑egg syndrome.
      Interpretation: Elevated Gal d 5 IgE confirms the diagnosis.
    - Test: Skin prick test to bird feathers
      Purpose: To demonstrate sensitization to bird allergens.
      When indicated: When respiratory symptoms on bird exposure are present.
      Interpretation: Positive test supports the diagnosis of bird‑related respiratory allergy.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Diagnostic for bird‑egg syndrome; explains the cross‑reactivity between bird feather allergens and egg yolk.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Periodic specialist review, similar to adult egg allergy; frequency not defined. Repeat specific IgE testing and reassessment of bird avoidance measures.
    Recommended tests:
      - Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      - Spirometry if asthma symptoms present
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent allergy to egg yolk and bird feather allergens
      - Risk of anaphylaxis with egg yolk ingestion
      - Need for bird avoidance and egg‑free diet
    Survivorship notes: This syndrome tends to persist lifelong. Patients must carry emergency medications and avoid egg yolk and bird exposure.

Egg allergy is an adverse immunological reaction, most often induced by the proteins in egg white, usually ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and/ or ovomucoid (Gal d 1) mediated by egg-specific IgE. - 7.2 | Egg-specific IgE


When skin prick testing is not available, measurement of eggspecific IgE may be carried out in patients with a history of moderate/severe reactions to egg containing food, to confirm a clinical suspicion of egg allergy. Low levels of egg-specific IgE may be found in children without clinical egg allergy.13 The measurement of egg-specific IgE in the absence of a history of egg ingestion is discouraged as, in this circumstance, the test has poor specificity and low negative predictive value; cautious home introduction or oral challenge will subsequently be required if the egg-specific IgE level is positive but low.8 Measurement of peanut-specific IgE should be included in infants with moderate/severe egg allergy to guide peanut allergy prevention advice.25

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Bird‑egg syndrome
  Synonyms:
    - Alpha‑livetin allergy
    - Egg yolk allergy with bird feather sensitization
  Description: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.
  Epidemiology: Rare; described mainly in adults, particularly women, with prolonged exposure to budgerigars, pigeons, or other caged birds.
  Clinical presentation: Upper and lower respiratory symptoms (rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma) on inhalation of bird allergens; gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Symptoms are triggered by ingestion of egg yolk, which contains high concentrations of alpha‑livetin. Onset typically after years of bird exposure.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To identify the characteristic cross‑reactivity between bird and egg allergens.
      When indicated: Suspected cases with respiratory symptoms on bird exposure and food reactions to egg yolk.
      Interpretation: A history of bird feather sensitivity and symptoms with egg (especially yolk) or chicken meat is highly suggestive.
    - Test: Skin prick test or specific IgE to egg yolk
      Purpose: To confirm sensitization to egg yolk proteins.
      When indicated: When bird‑egg syndrome is suspected.
      Interpretation: Positive test indicates sensitization to yolk allergen; further distinction can be made with component testing.
    - Test: Specific IgE to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify the specific cross‑reactive allergen.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected bird‑egg syndrome.
      Interpretation: Elevated Gal d 5 IgE confirms the diagnosis.
    - Test: Skin prick test to bird feathers
      Purpose: To demonstrate sensitization to bird allergens.
      When indicated: When respiratory symptoms on bird exposure are present.
      Interpretation: Positive test supports the diagnosis of bird‑related respiratory allergy.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Diagnostic for bird‑egg syndrome; explains the cross‑reactivity between bird feather allergens and egg yolk.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Periodic specialist review, similar to adult egg allergy; frequency not defined. Repeat specific IgE testing and reassessment of bird avoidance measures.
    Recommended tests:
      - Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      - Spirometry if asthma symptoms present
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent allergy to egg yolk and bird feather allergens
      - Risk of anaphylaxis with egg yolk ingestion
      - Need for bird avoidance and egg‑free diet
    Survivorship notes: This syndrome tends to persist lifelong. Patients must carry emergency medications and avoid egg yolk and bird exposure.

retrieved_chunks.text: ‘Bird egg syndrome’ was originally described in subjects, mainly women, who were sensitized to egg yolk and bird (budgerigar and hen) feathers.72 This syndrome is seen in subjects who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.73 The allergen responsible is alpha livetin (chicken serum albumin, Gal d 5), found in large amounts in egg yolk.74 Typically, patients develop upper and lower respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds and gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Egg yolk alpha-livetin (chicken serum albumin) is a cross-reactive allergen in the bird-egg syndrome. Chicken serum albumin (Gal d 5*) is a partially heatlabile inhalant and food allergen implicated in the bird-egg syndrome.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Bird‑egg syndrome
  Synonyms:
    - Alpha‑livetin allergy
    - Egg yolk allergy with bird feather sensitization
  Description: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.
  Epidemiology: Rare; described mainly in adults, particularly women, with prolonged exposure to budgerigars, pigeons, or other caged birds.
  Clinical presentation: Upper and lower respiratory symptoms (rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma) on inhalation of bird allergens; gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Symptoms are triggered by ingestion of egg yolk, which contains high concentrations of alpha‑livetin. Onset typically after years of bird exposure.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To identify the characteristic cross‑reactivity between bird and egg allergens.
      When indicated: Suspected cases with respiratory symptoms on bird exposure and food reactions to egg yolk.
      Interpretation: A history of bird feather sensitivity and symptoms with egg (especially yolk) or chicken meat is highly suggestive.
    - Test: Skin prick test or specific IgE to egg yolk
      Purpose: To confirm sensitization to egg yolk proteins.
      When indicated: When bird‑egg syndrome is suspected.
      Interpretation: Positive test indicates sensitization to yolk allergen; further distinction can be made with component testing.
    - Test: Specific IgE to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify the specific cross‑reactive allergen.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected bird‑egg syndrome.
      Interpretation: Elevated Gal d 5 IgE confirms the diagnosis.
    - Test: Skin prick test to bird feathers
      Purpose: To demonstrate sensitization to bird allergens.
      When indicated: When respiratory symptoms on bird exposure are present.
      Interpretation: Positive test supports the diagnosis of bird‑related respiratory allergy.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Diagnostic for bird‑egg syndrome; explains the cross‑reactivity between bird feather allergens and egg yolk.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Periodic specialist review, similar to adult egg allergy; frequency not defined. Repeat specific IgE testing and reassessment of bird avoidance measures.
    Recommended tests:
      - Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      - Spirometry if asthma symptoms present
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent allergy to egg yolk and bird feather allergens
      - Risk of anaphylaxis with egg yolk ingestion
      - Need for bird avoidance and egg‑free diet
    Survivorship notes: This syndrome tends to persist lifelong. Patients must carry emergency medications and avoid egg yolk and bird exposure.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Bird‑egg syndrome
  Synonyms:
    - Alpha‑livetin allergy
    - Egg yolk allergy with bird feather sensitization
  Description: A distinct form of egg allergy in which sensitization to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5), a protein abundant in egg yolk and bird feathers, leads to allergic symptoms upon ingestion of egg (especially yolk) and respiratory symptoms on exposure to birds. The syndrome is classically described in adults, predominantly women, who are exposed to caged birds or pigeons.
  Epidemiology: Rare; described mainly in adults, particularly women, with prolonged exposure to budgerigars, pigeons, or other caged birds.
  Clinical presentation: Upper and lower respiratory symptoms (rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma) on inhalation of bird allergens; gastrointestinal symptoms with chicken meat or lightly cooked eggs. Symptoms are triggered by ingestion of egg yolk, which contains high concentrations of alpha‑livetin. Onset typically after years of bird exposure.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To identify the characteristic cross‑reactivity between bird and egg allergens.
      When indicated: Suspected cases with respiratory symptoms on bird exposure and food reactions to egg yolk.
      Interpretation: A history of bird feather sensitivity and symptoms with egg (especially yolk) or chicken meat is highly suggestive.
    - Test: Skin prick test or specific IgE to egg yolk
      Purpose: To confirm sensitization to egg yolk proteins.
      When indicated: When bird‑egg syndrome is suspected.
      Interpretation: Positive test indicates sensitization to yolk allergen; further distinction can be made with component testing.
    - Test: Specific IgE to alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify the specific cross‑reactive allergen.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected bird‑egg syndrome.
      Interpretation: Elevated Gal d 5 IgE confirms the diagnosis.
    - Test: Skin prick test to bird feathers
      Purpose: To demonstrate sensitization to bird allergens.
      When indicated: When respiratory symptoms on bird exposure are present.
      Interpretation: Positive test supports the diagnosis of bird‑related respiratory allergy.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Diagnostic for bird‑egg syndrome; explains the cross‑reactivity between bird feather allergens and egg yolk.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Periodic specialist review, similar to adult egg allergy; frequency not defined. Repeat specific IgE testing and reassessment of bird avoidance measures.
    Recommended tests:
      - Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      - Spirometry if asthma symptoms present
    Long term effects:
      - Persistent allergy to egg yolk and bird feather allergens
      - Risk of anaphylaxis with egg yolk ingestion
      - Need for bird avoidance and egg‑free diet
    Survivorship notes: This syndrome tends to persist lifelong. Patients must carry emergency medications and avoid egg yolk and bird exposure.

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23. It is not standardized and there is a risk of severe reactions, so is not routinely recommended outside research settings. Skin prick testing using a slurry of baked egg had a high negative predictive value for a negative baked egg challenge in one study.24 It is not routinely used in clinical practice.

The objectives of this guidance are to increase global awareness of current concepts in the assessment and management of anaphylaxis in healthcare settings globally, to prevent anaphylaxis recurrences in the community, to reduce avoidable deaths, and to improve allocation of resources for anaphylaxis.

The World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance has been developed primarily for use by allergy/immunology specialists in countries without anaphylaxis guidelines and as an additional resource in areas where such guidelines are available. In addition, this will be a resource for other healthcare professionals who may encounter anaphylaxis patients in their settings. This includes primary care physicians, other medical specialties, and allied health staff caring for patients of any age, and in particular those who work in the emergency and peri-operative settings.

OA includes seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC), vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis (VKC and AKC) and contact blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC) (1). These clinical subtypes may be diagnosed and managed by ophthalmologists, allergists, pediatricians and rhinologists, with or without experience in managing allergies, considering clinical history and signs and symptoms, aided by in vivo and in vitro tests (1-3). Although several studies suggest a high co-morbidity of conjunctivitis and rhinitis, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians as a minor problem and sub-optimally treated. A recent survey revealed that daily treatment of OA has little concordance with current recommendations(4). Topical ocular decongestants and corticosteroids were used in the majority of cases. This was independent of the specific diagnosis of OA subtype and severity. Topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers, which

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature. Accepted Article

Methods General Search Strategy The literature search was based on the systematic literature search in Medline, SCOPUS and WebScience. First, we performed a SR of all SR and meta-analyses that addressed OA treatments, according to the search query. For each subtype of OA or treatment, if good quality SR or systematic analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were found, no further systematic search was performed. If no evidence or poor quality of evidence was found, a further systematic search was performed. The included literature was selected with respect to their hierarchy in the ‘evidence pyramid’. Eligibility Criteria We included SR of observational and interventional studies regarding treatment of OA (SAC, PAC, VKC, AKC and CBC).

That is why making the right diagnosis and starting VIT in a patient is so important. Routine diagnostic tests include skin prick tests (SPTs) and venom sIgE level determinationFigure 4. To avoid false negative results, the mentioned tests should be performed at least 2–4 weeks after the sting (the so-called refractory period) [30]. According to European guidelines, SPTs should be performed first. If their results are negative, the next step involves intradermal tests [30,31]. Intradermal tests have a much higher sensitivity than prick tests, which has been shown in clinical studies. SPTs identify 49% of patients with Hymenoptera venom allergy (HVA), whereas the combination of SPTs and intradermal tests made it possible to diagnose 94% of patients [32]. In Europe, standardized venoms of Apis mellifera, Vespula spp., Polistes spp. and Vespa crabro are available and can be used for skin tests. Moreover, skin tests have been shown to be safe, even in patients with mastocytosis [33,34]. Biomedicines 2022, 10, x FOR PEER REVIEW 5 of 16

The disadvantage of skin tests is that they are performed with venom extracts that may contain too little or even no allergen components at all. ### Should Allergists Routinely Investigate Hypersensitivity Reactions?

For patients with a history of HR to contrast media, the EAACI guidelines10 recommend skin prick and intradermal testing for both the suspected and alternative contrast agents, ideally 2 to 6months post-reaction. Negative results should be followed by a direct provocation challenge. Skin prick testing uses undiluted contrast (300-320mg/mL), while intradermal testing uses a 1:10 dilution. Various challenge protocols exist in the literature; a recent paper indicated a two-step challenge with 5 and 30mL dose separated by 15minutes can successfully identify patients potentially having an IgE-mediated reaction to contrast media.105 As outlined above, the evidence supporting various testing protocols are weak and unclear. Accurate positive predictive value assessments are difficult due to the rarity of severe reactions and limited patient reexposure data in patients with positive testing. While useful in rare cases (eg, severe reaction to unknown LOCM, or multiple contrast reactions), we do not recommend routine skin or intradermal testing over contrast switching due to weak supporting evidence and limited resources, though allergists with established protocols may still choose to use them.

For patients with a history of HR to contrast media, the EAACI guidelines10 recommend skin prick and intradermal testing for both the suspected and alternative contrast agents, ideally 2 to 6months post-reaction. Negative results should be followed by a direct provocation challenge. Skin prick testing uses undiluted contrast (300-320mg/mL), while intradermal testing uses a 1:10 dilution. Various challenge protocols exist in the literature; a recent paper indicated a two-step challenge with 5 and 30mL dose separated by 15minutes can successfully identify patients potentially having an IgE-mediated reaction to contrast media.105 As outlined above, the evidence supporting various testing protocols are weak and unclear. Accurate positive predictive value assessments are difficult due to the rarity of severe reactions and limited patient reexposure data in patients with positive testing. While useful in rare cases (eg, severe reaction to unknown LOCM, or multiple contrast reactions), we do not recommend routine skin or intradermal testing over contrast switching due to weak supporting evidence and limited resources, though allergists with established protocols may still choose to use them.

Allergic conjunctivitis is often comorbid with allergic rhinitis (AR) [14]. Therefore, when compared to AR, allergic conjunctivitis receives far less attention [7]. Once-daily ophthalmic medications are now available for allergic conjunctivitis [31, 37, 38], and this could foster adherence and treatment compliance. ## Key Messages: Implications for Clinical Practice

After reviewing the present situation of AC and its management with topical treatments, we can summarize some takehome messages for the practitioner:

- • Allergic conjunctivitis is prevalent and often underdiagnosed. - • An innovative multi-dose, preservative-free, antihistamine formulation (with HA) for once-daily treatment of allergic conjunctivitis has been recently developed. Summary Seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC) are the most frequent causes of ocular allergy (OA), and both conditions are underdiagnosed and undertreated. Therefore, its nosology includes seasonal allergic conjunctivitis (SAC) and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (PAC), depending on whether the specific aeroallergen is seasonal or permanent [1]. :(0123456789)

Allergic conjunctivitis is often comorbid with allergic rhinitis (AR) [14]. Therefore, when compared to AR, allergic conjunctivitis receives far less attention [7]. - • Allergic conjunctivitis is prevalent and often underdiagnosed. - • An innovative multi-dose, preservative-free, antihistamine formulation (with HA) for once-daily treatment of allergic conjunctivitis has been recently developed. Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_03
  Name: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis
  Synonyms:
    - VKC
  Description: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a persistent, chronic ocular allergic disorder with both IgE- and non-IgE-mediated mechanisms, often occurring in children and characterized by severe inflammation and potential corneal complications.
  Clinical presentation: Severe ocular itching, photophobia, tearing, mucous discharge, giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, and possible corneal involvement such as shield ulcers.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Ophthalmic examination
      Purpose: Assess conjunctival and corneal involvement (giant papillae, limbal infiltrates, corneal erosions).
      When indicated: Suspected VKC
    - Test: Allergy testing (skin prick or serum IgE)
      Purpose: Identify contributing allergens, although VKC may not be solely IgE-driven.
      When indicated: When allergic triggers are suspected.

retrieved_chunks.text:
The diagnosis of AC is based on clinical history, signs and symptoms, and confirmed with in vivo and in vitro allergen testing [16]. An exhaustive ocular examination to assess abnormalities of the conjunctiva, cornea, and tear film, together with collection of the patient’s clinical history should always be the first steps. Allergen-specific IgE response should be ascertained: the skin prick test (SPT), along with in vitro specific IgE measurement, is still considered the gold standard for this, although if the relationship between allergen exposure and ocular signs and symptoms is not clear, a conjunctival allergen provocation test may also be performed [1, 17]. ### Over‑the‑counter Medications

One important problem is that patients with ocular allergic disease often self-medicate; they purchase OTC medications and fail to seek help even when those therapies are ineffective [22, 23]. In one study [18], self-treatment measures were the first step taken by 56% of patients diagnosed with AC. Many OTC drugs are topical vasoconstrictors or decongestants that have limited efficacy in OA, as they do not treat the underlying cause of the disease [7]. Conversely, the use and overuse of OTC products may lead to adverse effects such as rebound vasodilation [23]. Furthermore, BAK is a very

common preservative in these solutions – present in over 70% of OTC eye drops – that, as mentioned, has the potential to induce ocular toxicity and exacerbate ocular surface damage [7].

### Should Allergists Routinely Investigate Hypersensitivity Reactions?

For patients with a history of HR to contrast media, the EAACI guidelines10 recommend skin prick and intradermal testing for both the suspected and alternative contrast agents, ideally 2 to 6months post-reaction. Negative results should be followed by a direct provocation challenge. Skin prick testing uses undiluted contrast (300-320mg/mL), while intradermal testing uses a 1:10 dilution. Various challenge protocols exist in the literature; a recent paper indicated a two-step challenge with 5 and 30mL dose separated by 15minutes can successfully identify patients potentially having an IgE-mediated reaction to contrast media.105 As outlined above, the evidence supporting various testing protocols are weak and unclear. Accurate positive predictive value assessments are difficult due to the rarity of severe reactions and limited patient reexposure data in patients with positive testing. While useful in rare cases (eg, severe reaction to unknown LOCM, or multiple contrast reactions), we do not recommend routine skin or intradermal testing over contrast switching due to weak supporting evidence and limited resources, though allergists with established protocols may still choose to use them.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_06
  Condition ref: cond_04
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with atopic keratoconjunctivitis
  Decision rules:
    - Initial management focuses on eyelid eczema and surface disease. Avoid triggers, maintain lid hygiene, use emollients. Oral antihistamines can be used for itching, and topical corticosteroids for acute flares.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: oral antihistamines
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Used to alleviate eyelid itching.
      Duration cycles: As needed.
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (low potency)
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Ointments or creams for acute eyelid eczema; low potency agents preferred.
      Duration cycles: Short courses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical calcineurin inhibitors (skin ointment 0.03% or 0.1%)
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Useful for lid eczema in AKC; burning sensation is common and secondary infections have been reported.
      Conditions for use: When corticosteroids are insufficient or to reduce steroid exposure.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: topical antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers
      Reason: Evidence for AKC is limited to case reports; not generally recommended.
  Supportive care:
    - Avoidance of irritants/sensitizing antigens.
    - Eyelid hygiene.
    - Emollients and skin moisturizing agents.
  Special considerations: AKC may require systemic immunosuppression in refractory cases with visual threat; cyclosporine is most commonly used, alternatives are tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil.

An exhaustive ocular examination to assess abnormalities of the conjunctiva, cornea, and tear film, together with collection of the patient’s clinical history should always be the first steps. Allergen-specific IgE response should be ascertained: the skin prick test (SPT), along with in vitro specific IgE measurement, is still considered the gold standard for this, although if the relationship between allergen exposure and ocular signs and symptoms is not clear, a conjunctival allergen provocation test may also be performed [1, 17]. ### Over‑the‑counter Medications

One important problem is that patients with ocular allergic disease often self-medicate; they purchase OTC medications and fail to seek help even when those therapies are ineffective [22, 23]. In one study [18], self-treatment measures were the first step taken by 56% of patients diagnosed with AC. Many OTC drugs are topical vasoconstrictors or decongestants that have limited efficacy in OA, as they do not treat the underlying cause of the disease [7]. Conversely, the use and overuse of OTC products may lead to adverse effects such as rebound vasodilation [23]. Furthermore, BAK is a very

common preservative in these solutions – present in over 70% of OTC eye drops – that, as mentioned, has the potential to induce ocular toxicity and exacerbate ocular surface damage [7]. ## Is There Room for Improvement in the Management of AC? AC continues to be an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease [7]. Considering the need for differential diagnosis, a multidisciplinary approach involving allergists, general practitioners, otolaryngologists, and eye care specialists is advisable [1, 17]. It should be borne in mind that in many settings, allergic conjunctivitis patients are often seen in primary care and, when referred to a specialist, those with SAC symptoms are usually referred to the allergist, while patients with PAC are more often referred to the ophthalmologist for differential diagnosis [1].

Skin prick testing using a slurry of baked egg had a high negative predictive value for a negative baked egg challenge in one study.24 It is not routinely used in clinical practice. - 7.2 | Egg-specific IgE


When skin prick testing is not available, measurement of eggspecific IgE may be carried out in patients with a history of moderate/severe reactions to egg containing food, to confirm a clinical suspicion of egg allergy. It is not possible to identify a cut-off for serum-specific IgE because of a lack of consistency between studies. Although there is a demonstrable relationship between serum IgE levels and challenge outcome within studies, there is poor agreement between centres.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: guideline_GUIDELINE - Leonardi et al. - 2019 - Management of ocular allergy
retrieved_chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_09
  Condition ref: cond_05
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with contact blepharoconjunctivitis
  Decision rules:
    - Identify and avoid the offending agent. Use lid hygiene and emollients. For acute eczema, low-potency topical corticosteroids can be applied.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (low potency)
      Summary: For acute phases of eyelid eczema; use low-potency agents such as hydrocortisone, desonide, triamcinolone acetonide.
      Duration cycles: Short courses during flares.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical calcineurin inhibitors (skin ointment 0.03% or 0.1%)
      Summary: Useful for lid eczema; tolerability may be limited by burning sensation.
      Conditions for use: When corticosteroids are insufficient or long-term use is needed.
  Supportive care:
    - Avoidance of identified allergens/irritants.
    - Eyelid hygiene.
    - Emollients and skin moisturizing agents.
  Special considerations: Secondary infections may occur with calcineurin inhibitor use, requiring vigilance.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_09
  Condition ref: cond_05
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with contact blepharoconjunctivitis
  Decision rules:
    - Identify and avoid the offending agent. Use lid hygiene and emollients. For acute eczema, low-potency topical corticosteroids can be applied.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (low potency)
      Summary: For acute phases of eyelid eczema; use low-potency agents such as hydrocortisone, desonide, triamcinolone acetonide.
      Duration cycles: Short courses during flares.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical calcineurin inhibitors (skin ointment 0.03% or 0.1%)
      Summary: Useful for lid eczema; tolerability may be limited by burning sensation.
      Conditions for use: When corticosteroids are insufficient or long-term use is needed.
  Supportive care:
    - Avoidance of identified allergens/irritants.
    - Eyelid hygiene.
    - Emollients and skin moisturizing agents.
  Special considerations: Secondary infections may occur with calcineurin inhibitor use, requiring vigilance.

The diagnosis of AC is based on clinical history, signs and symptoms, and confirmed with in vivo and in vitro allergen testing [16]. An exhaustive ocular examination to assess abnormalities of the conjunctiva, cornea, and tear film, together with collection of the patient’s clinical history should always be the first steps. Allergen-specific IgE response should be ascertained: the skin prick test (SPT), along with in vitro specific IgE measurement, is still considered the gold standard for this, although if the relationship between allergen exposure and ocular signs and symptoms is not clear, a conjunctival allergen provocation test may also be performed [1, 17]. ### Over‑the‑counter Medications

One important problem is that patients with ocular allergic disease often self-medicate; they purchase OTC medications and fail to seek help even when those therapies are ineffective [22, 23]. In one study [18], self-treatment measures were the first step taken by 56% of patients diagnosed with AC. Many OTC drugs are topical vasoconstrictors or decongestants that have limited efficacy in OA, as they do not treat the underlying cause of the disease [7]. Conversely, the use and overuse of OTC products may lead to adverse effects such as rebound vasodilation [23]. Furthermore, BAK is a very

common preservative in these solutions – present in over 70% of OTC eye drops – that, as mentioned, has the potential to induce ocular toxicity and exacerbate ocular surface damage [7].

The objectives of this guidance are to increase global awareness of current concepts in the assessment and management of anaphylaxis in healthcare settings globally, to prevent anaphylaxis recurrences in the community, to reduce avoidable deaths, and to improve allocation of resources for anaphylaxis.

The World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance has been developed primarily for use by allergy/immunology specialists in countries without anaphylaxis guidelines and as an additional resource in areas where such guidelines are available. In addition, this will be a resource for other healthcare professionals who may encounter anaphylaxis patients in their settings. This includes primary care physicians, other medical specialties, and allied health staff caring for patients of any age, and in particular those who work in the emergency and peri-operative settings.

gold_answer: This workgroup report examines the necessity of mandating stock epinephrine in all U.S. schools to ensure prompt treatment of anaphylaxis. It identifies ten barriers to adoption, including liability concerns and lack of training, and proposes strategies such as legal immunity, cost stabilization advocacy, and education. The report emphasizes that voluntary stock epinephrine laws may compromise student safety and advocates for mandated legislation supported by school nurse training and partnerships.

The objectives of this guidance are to increase global awareness of current concepts in the assessment and management of anaphylaxis in healthcare settings globally, to prevent anaphylaxis recurrences in the community, to reduce avoidable deaths, and to improve allocation of resources for anaphylaxis.

The World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance has been developed primarily for use by allergy/immunology specialists in countries without anaphylaxis guidelines and as an additional resource in areas where such guidelines are available. In addition, this will be a resource for other healthcare professionals who may encounter anaphylaxis patients in their settings. This includes primary care physicians, other medical specialties, and allied health staff caring for patients of any age, and in particular those who work in the emergency and peri-operative settings.

The current update was developed based on the previous guidelines,1 based on the best evidence available, such as that from systematic reviews performed to inform other guidelines,2 in the absence of randomized controlled trials3 with which to answer most clinical questions relevant to anaphylaxis. A first draft of the Guidance was compiled, and further discussed and refined through electronic correspondence and face-toface meetings. The updated draft was circulated to the WAO Board of Directors for review and comment. The Guidance was circulated to the WAO member societies for review, comments, and voting. Comments from responding organizations were evaluated and incorporated appropriately.

Special focus has been placed on regions in which national guidelines are lacking. All aspects have been assessed based on scientific evidence supporting statements. This guidance adopts the major indications from the previous anaphylaxis guidelines of the World Allergy Organization (WAO)1 and incorporates some slight changes in specific aspects such as the diagnostic criteria. The objectives of this guidance are to increase global awareness of current concepts in the assessment and management of anaphylaxis in healthcare settings globally, to prevent anaphylaxis recurrences in the community, to reduce avoidable deaths, and to improve allocation of resources for anaphylaxis. The World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance has been developed primarily for use by allergy/immunology specialists in countries without anaphylaxis guidelines and as an additional resource in areas where such guidelines are available. In addition, this will be a resource for other healthcare professionals who may encounter anaphylaxis patients in their settings. This includes primary care physicians, other medical specialties, and allied health staff caring for patients of any age, and in particular those who work in the emergency and peri-operative settings. The current update was developed based on the previous guidelines,1 based on the best evidence available, such as that from systematic reviews performed to inform other guidelines,2 in the absence of randomized controlled trials3 with which to answer most clinical questions relevant to anaphylaxis. A first draft of the Guidance was compiled, and further discussed and refined through electronic correspondence and face-toface meetings. retrieved_chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  - Pathway id: path_01
    Condition ref: cond_01
    Setting: first_line
    Patient population: Students and staff experiencing suspected anaphylaxis in the school setting, including those with known allergies and those without prior diagnosis
    Decision rules:
    - If signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis are present, administer epinephrine immediately and activate emergency medical services.
    - Use stock epinephrine if the individual does not have their own prescribed autoinjector or it is not available.
    Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Epinephrine autoinjector (e.g., EpiPen, Auvi-Q)
    Summary: Intramuscular injection of epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, to be administered promptly upon recognition.
    Key outcomes: Prompt epinephrine administration is associated with lower rates of mortality and near-fatality.
    Duration cycles: Single dose; may repeat every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist
    Not recommended:
    - Name: Delayed epinephrine administration or use of antihistamines as initial treatment
    Reason: Delays in epinephrine administration are linked to poorer outcomes; antihistamines do not effectively treat cardiovascular and respiratory symptoms of anaphylaxis.
    Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: After epinephrine administration
    Method: Monitor for improvement in respiratory distress, hypotension, and skin manifestations; continue emergency care until EMS arrival.
    Supportive care:
    - Position patient supine or in a position comfortable for breathing
    - Administer oxygen if available
    - Initiate CPR if indicated
    Special considerations: Stock epinephrine must be stored in unlocked, easily accessible locations; school personnel should receive training in anaphylaxis recognition and autoinjector use; legal immunity from liability for prescribers and staff is crucial for program implementation.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_04
  Condition ref: cond_02
  Setting: second_line
  Patient population: PAC patients with acute exacerbations, corneal involvement, or insufficient response to first-line therapy
  Decision rules:
    - If symptoms are not controlled with topical antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers or if corneal involvement occurs, consider adding a short course of topical corticosteroids under ophthalmologist supervision.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (short course)
      Summary: Used as short, pulsed therapy for acute exacerbations or corneal involvement, with close monitoring for side effects.
      Key outcomes: Rapid control of inflammation, but risk of increased intraocular pressure, cataract, and infection.
      Duration cycles: Short course; duration should be minimized.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical cyclosporine A 0.1%
      Summary: On-label in EU; used as a steroid-sparing agent in steroid-dependent patients, in specialized centers.
      Conditions for use: Steroid-dependent cases or when frequent corticosteroid use is required.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: tacrolimus 0.1% eye drops
      Reason: Reserved for severe VKC and AKC refractory to cyclosporine; off-label in EU for SAC/PAC.
  Supportive care:
    - Ophthalmologist monitoring for intraocular pressure and cataract formation during corticosteroid use.
  Special considerations: Corticosteroids should not be used as first-line in PAC due to safety concerns. They are reserved for severe or complicated cases.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: guideline_GUIDELINE - Cardona et al. - 2020 - World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020
retrieved_chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with suspected anaphylaxis, based on acute onset of symptoms involving skin/mucosal tissue plus respiratory compromise, cardiovascular instability, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or acute hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after known allergen exposure.
  Decision rules:
    - Immediately remove suspected trigger if possible (e.g., discontinue drug infusion).
    - Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin.
    - Call for emergency medical services simultaneously.
    - Inject epinephrine (adrenaline) intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh).
    - Position patient: supine unless respiratory distress (then sitting); if pregnant, left lateral semi-recumbent; if unconscious, recovery position.
    - Repeat intramuscular epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms refractory.
    - If respiratory distress, administer high-flow oxygen (100% non-rebreather mask) and consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway obstruction or inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists for bronchoconstriction (not as substitute for epinephrine).
    - If cardiovascular instability, establish IV access with wide-bore cannula, give IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg crystalloid), and consider IV epinephrine infusion under expert monitoring if refractory.
    - Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm, and respiratory status frequently; observe for biphasic reaction (at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions).
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer 0.01 mg/kg body weight (maximum 0.5 mg per dose) into the antero-lateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed to control symptoms.
      Duration cycles: Until symptoms resolve; may require multiple doses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Intravenous epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion
      Summary: For anaphylaxis refractory to repeated intramuscular epinephrine. Must be administered by experienced personnel with cardiac monitoring, preferably as an infusion via pump. Various low-dose protocols exist (e.g., Brown et al. protocol).
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis with ongoing cardiovascular or respiratory compromise despite appropriate intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: Consider for upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal edema) as an adjunct to intramuscular epinephrine.
      Conditions for use: Signs of upper airway obstruction (stridor). Not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol)
      Summary: Adjuvant for bronchoconstriction symptoms after epinephrine administration.
      Conditions for use: Persistent bronchospasm despite epinephrine.
    - Name: H1-antihistamines (second-generation oral or first-generation parenteral)
      Summary: May help relieve cutaneous symptoms (e.g., urticaria, pruritus). Limited role; should not delay epinephrine administration. Parenteral first-generation agents (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, clemastine) available; rapid IV administration can cause hypotension. Some guidelines consider them third-line.
      Conditions for use: Symptomatic relief of skin manifestations only, after epinephrine.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids (e.g., intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone)
      Summary: Historically used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, especially in asthmatic patients. Increasing evidence questions benefit; routine use controversial.
      Conditions for use: Consider in moderate-severe anaphylaxis, particularly with asthma, after epinephrine. Not for acute rescue.
    - Name: Glucagon
      Summary: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis not optimally responding to epinephrine, especially those on beta-blockers. Evidence limited.
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blockers.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Intravenous bolus epinephrine
      Reason: Risk of fatal arrhythmias; intravenous route should not be used for initial treatment and only as infusion under expert monitoring.
    - Name: Antihistamines as first-line therapy
      Reason: Do not replace epinephrine; they have a limited role and may delay life-saving epinephrine administration.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids as sole acute treatment
      Reason: No evidence of benefit in acute anaphylaxis management; routine use is controversial and may be harmful.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Throughout acute management
      Method: Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status.
      Interpretation: Reassess for resolution of symptoms or signs of biphasic reaction. Biphasic reactions may occur within 6-12 hours after initial reaction.
    - Timepoint: After initial treatment and stabilization
      Method: Observation period of at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions or those requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
      Interpretation: Ensure no recurrence before discharge; educate patient on risk of biphasic reaction and indications to return.
  Supportive care:
    - High flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) for respiratory distress or patients receiving repeated epinephrine.
    - Intravenous access with wide-bore cannula (14 or 16 gauge in adults).
    - Intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) for cardiovascular instability.
    - Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous cardiac compressions if indicated.
    - Positioning: supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress); left lateral semi-recumbent if pregnant; recovery position if unconscious.
  Special considerations: Pregnant patients: position in left lateral semi-recumbent. Patients on beta-blockers: may require glucagon for refractory symptoms. Self-management: patients at risk should carry epinephrine auto-injector and have a written emergency action plan; instruct on when and how to self-administer epinephrine into the antero-lateral thigh.

retrieved_chunks.document_id: guideline_GUIDELINE - Cardona et al. - 2020 - World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020
retrieved_chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with suspected anaphylaxis, based on acute onset of symptoms involving skin/mucosal tissue plus respiratory compromise, cardiovascular instability, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or acute hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after known allergen exposure.
  Decision rules:
    - Immediately remove suspected trigger if possible (e.g., discontinue drug infusion).
    - Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin.
    - Call for emergency medical services simultaneously.
    - Inject epinephrine (adrenaline) intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh).
    - Position patient: supine unless respiratory distress (then sitting); if pregnant, left lateral semi-recumbent; if unconscious, recovery position.
    - Repeat intramuscular epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms refractory.
    - If respiratory distress, administer high-flow oxygen (100% non-rebreather mask) and consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway obstruction or inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists for bronchoconstriction (not as substitute for epinephrine).
    - If cardiovascular instability, establish IV access with wide-bore cannula, give IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg crystalloid), and consider IV epinephrine infusion under expert monitoring if refractory.
    - Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm, and respiratory status frequently; observe for biphasic reaction (at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions).
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer 0.01 mg/kg body weight (maximum 0.5 mg per dose) into the antero-lateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed to control symptoms.
      Duration cycles: Until symptoms resolve; may require multiple doses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Intravenous epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion
      Summary: For anaphylaxis refractory to repeated intramuscular epinephrine. Must be administered by experienced personnel with cardiac monitoring, preferably as an infusion via pump. Various low-dose protocols exist (e.g., Brown et al. protocol).
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis with ongoing cardiovascular or respiratory compromise despite appropriate intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: Consider for upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal edema) as an adjunct to intramuscular epinephrine.
      Conditions for use: Signs of upper airway obstruction (stridor). Not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol)
      Summary: Adjuvant for bronchoconstriction symptoms after epinephrine administration.
      Conditions for use: Persistent bronchospasm despite epinephrine.
    - Name: H1-antihistamines (second-generation oral or first-generation parenteral)
      Summary: May help relieve cutaneous symptoms (e.g., urticaria, pruritus). Limited role; should not delay epinephrine administration. Parenteral first-generation agents (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, clemastine) available; rapid IV administration can cause hypotension. Some guidelines consider them third-line.
      Conditions for use: Symptomatic relief of skin manifestations only, after epinephrine.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids (e.g., intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone)
      Summary: Historically used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, especially in asthmatic patients. Increasing evidence questions benefit; routine use controversial.
      Conditions for use: Consider in moderate-severe anaphylaxis, particularly with asthma, after epinephrine. Not for acute rescue.
    - Name: Glucagon
      Summary: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis not optimally responding to epinephrine, especially those on beta-blockers. Evidence limited.
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blockers.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Intravenous bolus epinephrine
      Reason: Risk of fatal arrhythmias; intravenous route should not be used for initial treatment and only as infusion under expert monitoring.
    - Name: Antihistamines as first-line therapy
      Reason: Do not replace epinephrine; they have a limited role and may delay life-saving epinephrine administration.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids as sole acute treatment
      Reason: No evidence of benefit in acute anaphylaxis management; routine use is controversial and may be harmful.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Throughout acute management
      Method: Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status.
      Interpretation: Reassess for resolution of symptoms or signs of biphasic reaction. Biphasic reactions may occur within 6-12 hours after initial reaction.
    - Timepoint: After initial treatment and stabilization
      Method: Observation period of at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions or those requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
      Interpretation: Ensure no recurrence before discharge; educate patient on risk of biphasic reaction and indications to return.
  Supportive care:
    - High flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) for respiratory distress or patients receiving repeated epinephrine.
    - Intravenous access with wide-bore cannula (14 or 16 gauge in adults).
    - Intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) for cardiovascular instability.
    - Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous cardiac compressions if indicated.
    - Positioning: supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress); left lateral semi-recumbent if pregnant; recovery position if unconscious.
  Special considerations: Pregnant patients: position in left lateral semi-recumbent. Patients on beta-blockers: may require glucagon for refractory symptoms. Self-management: patients at risk should carry epinephrine auto-injector and have a written emergency action plan; instruct on when and how to self-administer epinephrine into the antero-lateral thigh.
